source.title: Model Collapse Demystified: The Case of Regression
source.authors: Elvis Dohmatob; Yunzhen Feng; Julia Kempe

record.tranche_reason: The study derives and experimentally examines how recursively generated training data modifies regression scaling laws, refining the claim that scaling behavior carries over unchanged across training regimes.
record.gate_note: The study does not sweep language-model parameter count, training tokens, or compute, or compare architectures. Results it cites about scaling laws in other papers are not extracted. The reported regression and kernel-regression results below bear on recursive synthetic-data training and setup-dependent scaling.
record.test_reason: The study analyses ridge and kernel ridge regression on Gaussian-design and MNIST-regression data. It derives and simulates how test error scales with sample size T when labels come from recursively fitted generators. It trains no language, image or other neural models and sweeps no parameters, tokens or compute. It cites Kaplan and Hoffmann only as motivation. Its scaling results concern a different kind of system, a classical kernel regression proxy, so no row measures what any version names. The model-collapse scaling results are recorded under fits_no_version rather than as a test of V5 or V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially right. The authors conclude that recursive training on synthetic labels modifies the usual test-error scaling laws in high-dimensional ridge and kernel regression. Error grows with the number of generations and can plateau or diverge, and the optimal regularization changes. They validate this on simulated data and MNIST kernel regression. The results are framed as theory for regression, with only speculative implications for LLMs.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses theoretical analysis of Gaussian-design linear and kernel regression, plus regression experiments, rather than language-model parameter/token/compute sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The results vary with the synthetic-data generation process, generator sample size, number of generations, noise, covariance spectrum, and regularization exponent. The over-parameterized results also distinguish repeated from independent design matrices.

fits_no_version.finding: Recursive synthetic-label training adds an n-proportional term to ridge-regression test error. The power-law rate in T changes, and the error can plateau at about n*sigma0^2/T0 (low-dimensional case, Fig. 1) or diverge under the clean-data regularization exponent (Figs. 2, 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In kernel/ridge regression with power-law spectra, training on recursively generated labels modifies the data-scaling law of test error, slowing it, plateauing it or making it diverge, and shifts the optimal regularization exponent.

record.problems: The experiments use regression and kernel regression rather than language models; plotted values are not numerically reported in the text. Simulated experiments use 10 repetitions, and the MNIST experiment is a constructed regression task.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 1's isotropic-covariance curves and Figure 3's over-parameterized bias results concern collapse behavior but do not directly report the scaling-law results catalogued here. Other cited studies' findings are excluded.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss sweep over parameters, tokens or compute for language models.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No neural models in other modalities or regimes. Only kernel and linear ridge regression on synthetic and MNIST-regression data.
No comparison of fitting choices, parameter counting or published laws for neural models.

missing.what: In the low-dimensional unregularized case, the test-error scaling changes from sigma^2/T to sigma^2/T + n*sigma0^2/T0, a plateau visible in simulations.
In the noisy regime, the rate is T^-(gamma-1/(2*beta*r+1)) with gamma=min(1,b-a), and it vanishes only if b > a+1/(2*beta*r+1).

record.verdict_notes: The reader tagged V5/V7 as tested at T5. That was reversed because the system is classical ridge/kernel regression, not the kind of model the versions name, and the scaling variable is regression sample size. If the phenomenon's curators treat kernel-regression scaling theory as in scope for V5, R3-R5 would read as limits_scope for the synthetic-data regime under the clean-data exponent. The corrected exponent l* still yields a slower power law, per Cor. 5.3.

versions.untested_parts: No language-model loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fit is used to predict much larger language-model runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between model parameters and training tokens.
No comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Tests recursive synthetic-data training in linear and kernel regression, not image/video models or fine-tuning and transfer more broadly.
No downstream language-model task performance or relationship to pretraining loss.

Tests changes associated with synthetic-data training and regularization in regression; does not compare parameter-counting conventions or fitting methods, or establish why published language-model laws disagree.

rows.subject: Downstream ridge predictor
rows.stage_stated: trained on recursively generated synthetic labels
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 5.2 derives test-error scaling for power-law covariance spectra with adaptive ridge regularization.
rows.baseline: Clean-data scaling is described as Bias + Var ≍ T^-2ℓr + σ²T^-(1-ℓ/β).
rows.note: The result gives a scaling law but adds a synthetic-data term and changes the clean-data rate; it is a regression result, not a language-model scaling test.
rows.check: This is an analytic theorem (Thm 5.2) for ridge regression in the RMT limit, not a measured loss of a neural or other model of the kind V5 names. Versions V5/V7 do not apply.

rows.subject: Downstream ridge predictor
rows.stage_stated: trained on recursively generated synthetic labels
rows.operation_detail: Corollary 5.3 derives the regularization exponent and test-error rate minimizing error in the synthetic-data setting.

conditions.value: power-law covariance; T0 ≍ T^b; n ≍ T^a

rows.measure: Optimal regularization exponent and held-out test-error rate
rows.baseline: Clean-data fast rate Etest ≍ T^-2βr; clean-data exponent ℓcrit = β/(2βr + 1).
rows.value: ℓ⋆ = min((b-a)ℓcrit, β); optimal test error ≍ T^-(b-a)c.
rows.note: The optimal exponent and rate depend on the synthetic-data setting; the study describes a crossover to a slower rate.
rows.check: This is an analytic corollary (Cor 5.3) on the optimal ridge exponent, l* = min((b-a)l_crit, beta). It concerns regularization tuning in kernel regression, not model scaling, so it is not a V5/V7 measurement.

rows.subject: Kernel ridge regression
rows.stage_stated: trained on recursively generated synthetic data
rows.operation_detail: Figure 2 compares test error across sample sizes and generations using adaptive regularization.

conditions.value: λ = T^-ℓcrit from the clean-data setting

rows.measure: Test error as sample size T changes
rows.baseline: Clean-data setting and its regularization choice ℓcrit.
rows.value: The text states that test error diverges with sample size T under the clean-data choice; a corrected exponent is proposed for synthetic data.
rows.note: The plotted values are not transcribed; the text explicitly describes divergence under the clean-data regularization choice.
rows.check: This is a simulated linear ridge regression with d=300 (Fig. 2, right). Test error diverges with T only under the clean-data exponent l_crit; the corrected exponent is proposed to avoid this. It is not a model-scaling result for any version.

rows.subject: Kernel ridge regression
rows.stage_stated: trained on recursively generated synthetic data
rows.operation_detail: Figure 5 reports test error across sample sizes for the RBF-kernel MNIST regression experiment.
rows.measure: Test error as sample size T changes
rows.baseline: Generation n = 0 is the clean-data reference.
rows.value: The text states that the effect of fake data makes test error non-decreasing in T.
rows.uncertainty: Error bars from 10 repetitions; no numerical interval stated.
rows.note: The caption and text describe the trend; values are only plotted.
rows.check: This is RBF kernel ridge regression on MNIST converted to regression. Test error is non-decreasing in T for fake-data generations (Fig. 5 caption). Values are plot-only, and the system is not one the versions name.
